chunks: Inductor continuity vs motor inrush. The question: Inductors oppose instantaneous changes in current, but motors/solenoid still experience very fast and large inrush currents.
Why is this?
An inductor is a coil that resists sudden changes in current. It does not cap how big the current gets, and it does not hold the current at zero for long.
It only controls how fast the current can change.
So a motor's starting surge is not a contradiction: the current does start at zero and rise smoothly, but it rises very fast, to a very large value.
Think of a heavy flywheel on a car engine. It cannot jump to full speed instantly, so it takes a moment to get going. But it does not decide the top speed. The engine does.
The inductor is the flywheel: it sets how fast the current ramps. The winding resistance and the missing back-EMF set the final value.
The analogy has one gap: the electrical ramp is far faster than anything mechanical.
Both curves start at zero with the same slope (12 amps/ms). The locked-rotor current heads to 6 amps. The free rotor peaks near 5 amps at about 1.
3 milliseconds, then decays toward zero as back-EMF builds over a few mechanical time constants (this plot has no friction; a real motor settles at its no-load current, about 0.
1 amps here). The inrush is a spike lasting a few milliseconds.
Inductance ( L ): how strongly a coil resists changes in current, in henries. Time constant ( L over R ): the time scale of the current's rise.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply. Inrush: the large current right after turn-on.
Mechanical time constant: how long the rotor (the spinning part) takes to speed up.
A 12 volts motor has a 2 ohms winding and 1 millihenries of inductance. The final current at standstill is V over R = 12 volts / 2 ohms = 6 amps .
The time constant is 1 millihenries / 2 ohms = 0. 5 milliseconds. So the current climbs to about 63% of 6 amps in half a millisecond.
The rotor needs milliseconds to tens of milliseconds to build back-EMF, so the current reaches nearly 6 amps first.
That is the whole idea: the inductor sets the ramp rate, and the resistance sets the peak.
"Inductors don't limit how large the current gets, only how fast it changes: v equals L di over dt . So the current starts at zero and ramps at V over L .
A motor winding has tiny L , so that's thousands of amps per second. At standstill there's no back-EMF, so the final current is just V over R , many times the running current.
It rises with a time constant L over R of about a millisecond, far faster than the rotor can speed up and build back-EMF. That's the inrush."
